name: vpmdhaj
iocPatterns: Malicious npm package names with typosquatting such as @vpmdhaj/elastic-helper
Suspicious preinstall/postinstall lifecycle hook URLs pointing to aab.sportsontheweb.net or obfuscator.io
HTTP requests containing the custom header X‑Supply: 1 to command and control domains
Downloads of the Bun runtime from https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases during installation
Usage of AWS IMDSv2, ECS task metadata APIs and STS GetCallerIdentity/AssumeRole patterns
Exfiltration of Vault tokens or Secrets Manager secrets across multiple regions
keyCapabilities: Supply chain attack via the npm ecosystem
Typosquatting on well‑known OpenSearch and Elastic packages
Exploitation of npm lifecycle hooks (preinstall/postinstall) for automatic execution
Two‑stage staging: HTTP C2 beacon or Bun runtime loader
Credential harvesting of AWS (IMDSv2, ECS task role, Secrets Manager), HashiCorp Vault tokens, GitHub Actions secrets and npm publish tokens
Persistence through re‑spawning the payload on module require() calls
Downstream supply chain pivoting via stolen npm publish credentials
recommendedActions: Implement strict npm package whitelists and disallow preinstall/postinstall scripts without explicit approval.
Configure alerting for high‑numbered versions and typosquatted package names in the npm registry.
Block outbound HTTP/HTTPS traffic to known malicious domains such as aab.sportsontheweb.net during npm installs.
Restrict VM access to AWS IMDSv2 and enforce least‑privilege IAM roles for build agents.
Rotate credentials stored in HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GitHub Actions, and npm publish tokens on a regular schedule.
Sandbox Bun runtime downloads unless explicitly authorized by the security team.
Monitor CI/CD logs for unexpected outbound connections and suspicious process creation.
Pin verified package versions and avoid automatic upgrades until validated.
campaignsText: vpmdhaj’s activity illustrates a fast‑paced, opportunistic campaign that relies on mass typosquatting to compromise developers’ trust in npm dependencies. The attacker’s pattern of rapidly publishing dozens of malicious packages indicates an emphasis on quantity and speed over stealth. Victims are diverse, spanning finance, healthcare, manufacturing, aviation, defense, hospitality and energy industries, often using cloud‑native CI/CD pipelines. Notable behaviors include the reuse of legitimate public repositories (e.g., GitHub releases) for staging payloads and sophisticated credential harvesting that facilitates both horizontal expansion within a single environment and lateral movement across multiple cloud accounts.
description: The threat actor vpmdhaj executed a rapid supply‑chain attack by publishing 14 typosquatted npm packages that leveraged preinstall/postinstall lifecycle hooks to harvest AWS, HashiCorp Vault, GitHub Actions and npm publish credentials. The payload was delivered via an HTTP C2 beacon or an injected Bun runtime loader, enabling lateral movement and downstream compromise of cloud and CI/CD infrastructures. The operation appears financially motivated and targets high‑value cloud environments across multiple industries.
goals: vpmdhaj’s strategic objective is primarily financial gain through the acquisition of cloud credentials that enable rapid expansion into downstream supply‑chain victims. By targeting npm packages associated with OpenSearch, ElasticSearch and related DevOps libraries, the actor exploits trusted developer pipelines to inject malicious code that steals AWS IAM roles, Vault tokens, GitHub Actions secrets and npm publish tickets. The attacker then capitalizes on these identities to move laterally within cloud environments, exfiltrate data or modify CI/CD processes to create persistent footholds across sectors such as financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, energy, aviation and hospitality.
